At the back of the kitchen drawer lives a key that opens nothing we own. It is brass, with a square head and one tooth worn almost smooth. Whenever we move, somebody holds it up and asks the sensible question. Then somebody else says, “Better keep it,” and into the box it goes.

I used to think this was a failure of housekeeping. Now I rather like the arrangement. Nearly everything in our house has to justify its place. The kettle boils, the lamp shines, the little rubber wedge prevents the bathroom door from swinging shut. Even the chipped blue bowl earns its shelf by holding lemons. The key alone has retired on a pension.

Last winter my niece found it while looking for birthday candles. She asked what it opened. I told her the truth: I didn't know. This delighted her. She spent the afternoon testing possibilities, not just locks but knots in wood, cracks between floorboards, and the narrow mouth of a ceramic fish. At dinner she announced that the key belonged to a house that hadn't been built yet.

She put it back beside the string.

Yesterday the drawer stuck halfway open. I reached behind it and felt around until my fingers closed on the obstruction. It was the key, standing upright, its square head caught against the frame. I laid it flat and pushed the drawer shut. For the first time in thirty years, I knew exactly what the thing had done, and already I missed the mystery.
